title: Version Control (Git)
description: Team workflows and the Git tools for rewriting and investigating history.
resumo: Git Flow for planned releases; GitHub Flow or trunk-based for continuous delivery — keep branches short.
`rebase -i --autosquash` cleans your branch before the PR; push with `--force-with-lease`, never `--force`.
Cherry-pick hotfixes from main to the release branch with `-x` — and never leave a fix only on the release.
Reflog keeps 90 days (30 for unreachable commits) — check it before deleting and re-cloning.
`git bisect run` finds the bad commit automatically; exit 125 skips commits that do not build.

subsections.subtitle: Branching Strategies
subsections.description: Git Flow, GitHub Flow and trunk-based development.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** without an agreed branching model, everyone integrates differently: branches that live for months, releases that need a week of merging.

**Concept:** Git Flow uses long-lived branches (main, develop, release, hotfix) and fits planned releases, but leads to big merges and late integration. GitHub Flow is simpler: main is always deployable, and short feature branches go in through pull requests. Trunk-based development goes further: everyone integrates into the trunk several times a day, with feature flags hiding unfinished work — the model that fits CI/CD best.

**How it works:** most teams doing continuous delivery use GitHub Flow or trunk-based development. The key in all of them: keep branches short.
examples.code:
# GitHub Flow
git switch -c feature/cancel-order
# ... small commits ...
git push -u origin feature/cancel-order
# open PR -> review -> CI green -> merge into main -> deploy

# Git Flow (summary)
# main <- release/1.4 <- develop <- feature/*
# main <- hotfix/1.4.1
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between Git Flow, GitHub Flow and trunk-based development?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A feature branch that lives for weeks. main keeps moving, and the final merge brings huge conflicts and bugs found too late. Merge small slices often, hiding unfinished parts behind a feature flag.
examples.code:
# WRONG: a branch alive for 6 weeks
main      A---B---C---D---E---F---G---H
feature    \---1---2---3---4---5---6      -> giant merge, conflicts, late bugs

# RIGHT: small slices merged daily; unfinished parts behind a feature flag

subsections.subtitle: Interactive Rebase, Squash and Fixup
subsections.description: A clean history before the pull request.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** your branch has twelve commits: "wip", "fix", "fix again", "typo". Reviewers have to read the history of your mistakes instead of the change.

**Concept:** `git rebase -i` lets you reorder, edit, combine (squash or fixup) and drop local commits, turning a pile of "WIP" commits into a few coherent ones. `git commit --fixup=<hash>` marks a commit as a correction of an earlier one, and `--autosquash` folds it in automatically. Rebase rewrites hashes, so never do it on branches other people already use (such as main).

**How it works:** on your own feature branch, after rewriting, push with `--force-with-lease`.
examples.code:
git commit --fixup=a1b2c3d          # marks a fix for an earlier commit
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main

# In the editor:
# pick   a1b2c3d feat: order cancellation
# fixup  e4f5a6b fixup! feat: order cancellation
# reword 9c8d7e6 test: cover cancellation

git push --force-with-lease
examples.interview_question: When should you avoid rebasing shared branches?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Pushing a rewritten branch with plain `--force`. If a teammate pushed to your branch in the meantime, their commits are overwritten without warning. `--force-with-lease` refuses when the remote has commits you have not seen.
examples.code:
# WRONG: silently discards anything pushed since your last fetch
git push --force

# RIGHT
git push --force-with-lease

subsections.subtitle: Cherry-pick and Hotfixes
subsections.description: Bringing one specific fix to another branch.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a bug fix is on main, but release 1.4 is in production and needs the fix now — without the unreleased features that are also on main.

**Concept:** `git cherry-pick` applies one specific commit to another branch, creating a new commit with the same changes. It is the usual way to bring a hotfix from main to a release branch. `-x` records the origin in the message. Use it sparingly: frequent cherry-picks duplicate commits and cause repeated conflicts.

**How it works:** in a conflict, resolve it, `git add`, then `git cherry-pick --continue`.
examples.code:
git switch release/1.4
git cherry-pick -x 3f9a2b1            # bring the hotfix made on main
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d..f6e5d4c      # a range of commits
# On conflict: resolve, git add, git cherry-pick --continue
examples.interview_question: When is cherry-pick a good solution?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Fixing directly on the release branch and never bringing the fix back to main. The next release is cut from main — and the bug returns. Fix on main first and cherry-pick to the release, or merge the release branch back.
examples.code:
# WRONG: the fix exists only on release/1.4
git switch release/1.4 && git commit -m "fix: tax rounding"
# release 1.5 is cut from main -> the bug is back

# RIGHT
git switch main && git commit -m "fix: tax rounding"
git switch release/1.4 && git cherry-pick -x <hash>

subsections.subtitle: Reflog: Recovering "Lost" Work
subsections.description: Undoing a reset, a bad rebase or a deleted branch.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a `git reset --hard` or a rebase went wrong, and the commits seem to be gone.

**Concept:** the reflog records every move of `HEAD` in your local repository — commits, checkouts, resets, rebases. By default entries stay 90 days, and 30 days for commits that became unreachable (like the ones "lost" in a reset). Find the earlier state and go back to it, or create a branch from it. It also recovers a branch deleted before pushing.

**How it works:** the reflog cannot help with changes that were never committed — commit early, even as WIP.
examples.code:
git reflog
# 3f9a2b1 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
# c7d8e9f HEAD@{1}: commit: feat: sales report

git reset --hard HEAD@{1}                  # back to the earlier state
git switch -c recovered c7d8e9f            # or create a branch from it
examples.interview_question: How do you recover commits after an accidental git reset --hard?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Deleting the folder and cloning again to "fix" a broken repository. The reflog is local: the fresh clone has none, and your unpushed commits are gone for good. Look at `git reflog` first.
examples.code:
# WRONG
rm -rf shop-api && git clone git@github.com:shop/api.git    # local commits lost

# RIGHT
git reflog                      # find the good state
git reset --hard HEAD@{2}

subsections.subtitle: Git Bisect
subsections.description: A binary search for the commit that introduced a bug.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** something that worked in version 1.3 is broken now, and there are 300 commits in between.

**Concept:** `git bisect` runs a binary search over the history: you mark one good and one bad commit, and Git checks out the middle for you to test. In about log₂(N) steps — 9 for 300 commits — the culprit appears. With `git bisect run` and a test script, the whole search is automatic: exit code 0 means good, 1–127 means bad, and 125 means "skip this commit".

**How it works:** finish with `git bisect reset` to return to where you started.
examples.code:
git bisect start
git bisect bad                   # the current commit has the bug
git bisect good v1.3.0           # this version worked
# test each step and mark it: git bisect good | git bisect bad

# Automatic: the script exits 0 (good) or non-zero (bad)
git bisect run ./mvnw -q test -Dtest=CheckoutTest
git bisect reset
examples.interview_question: How do you quickly find the commit that broke a feature?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A bisect script that returns 1 when the project does not compile. Commits that simply do not build are marked bad, and bisect blames the wrong commit. Exit 125 to skip those.
examples.code:
#!/bin/sh
# bisect-test.sh
./mvnw -q compile || exit 125           # does not build: skip this commit
./mvnw -q test -Dtest=CheckoutTest      # 0 = good, 1 = bad

git bisect run ./bisect-test.sh
